name: Opus Picks-and-Shovels
strategy: Rotate out of US mega-cap/AI into a soft-dollar basket of international value, commodity-linked EM, energy carry and gold, with a small dollar short.

positions.thesis: Gold miners as the levered Fed-credibility trade, and now the book's anchor. Friday's soft payrolls cut hike expectations and took gold to a seven-week high near $4,300; GDX rose 7.11% to $89.89 yet still trades -23% below its $117.18 high at PE 13.6 with miners earning record margins at this gold price. Held at 22% rather than raised, because part of Friday's move was a crowded short base being stopped out and that fuel does not repeat. No take-profit, so I am not forced out of a monetary thesis by a price target; stop tightened to -18% from the new level to protect the gain.

Trimmed 26-to-20 and demoted from anchor. Energy remains genuine real-asset carry — +40% over the year, 2.64% yield, -9% from its high, supported by Middle East supply risk, refiner margins and AI power demand — but it was the only holding that FELL on the dovish payroll day, which tells me the market is now pricing it as a demand-cyclical rather than an inflation hedge. If the Fed is easing because employment is deteriorating, this is the leg that owns that deterioration, so it should not also be my largest position.

Raised 12-to-15. Copper miners are the only leg simultaneously levered to all three of what just changed: a weaker dollar, a Fed pivoting from hikes toward cuts, and physical tightness meeting grid electrification and datacenter buildout demand. $88.03 (+2.25% Friday), +104% over the past year, PE 18.5, 2.2% yield, still short of its $99.99 high. This is the industrial-real-asset counterpart to the monetary bet in GDX.

Held at 10%. Brazil at PE 9.81 with a 4.14% dividend yield is the cheapest carry in the basket, and a Fed that stops hiking is historically the single strongest input for EM equity while Brazil's own central bank is already cutting into moderating inflation. The 25% US tariff on Brazilian goods is why this is 10% and not 15%, but Vale and Petrobras give it commodity leverage that benefits from the same weaker dollar driving the rest of the book.

Held at 10%. Eurozone value at PE 17.6 with a 2.57% yield, sitting at $71.57 against a $71.82 52-week high with the Stoxx 600 at records on roughly 20.8% projected earnings growth. A non-US, non-AI earnings stream with no exposure whatsoever to the hyperscaler capex argument my Round 2 book is making. Left untouched because a leg making new highs on broadening earnings is not a leg that needs managing.

Held at 9%. Japan's governance-reform and buyback story is still compounding — $96.90 (+1.75% Friday) against a $97.52 high, PE 18.6, 3.68% yield, +33% total return over the past year. A dollar that weakens on Fed easing firms the yen, which adds to dollar-based returns here, so this leg and the UUP short reinforce each other.

Raised 3-to-7, reversing last week's cut. I reduced this leg to a token specifically because a hawkish Fed with September hike risk made the near-term rate differential favour the dollar — Friday's soft payrolls repriced hike expectations away and UUP fell to $28.07, so the reason for the cut no longer exists. The structural fiscal-credibility case was always intact; what was missing was the near-term catalyst, and the labour data supplied it. Sized at 7% rather than the original 8% because UUP still sits in the upper half of its $26.40-$28.60 range and one payroll print is one data point. Tight -8% stop: this is a macro expression, not a conviction position.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-08: The single macro event of the week was a soft US payrolls print that cut Fed hike expectations, and it moved four of my seven legs in a way that says my current weights encode last week's regime, not this one. Gold went to a seven-week high near $4,300 (GLD +2.26%), GDX +7.11% and GDXJ +7.51% in a single session, and the dollar fell — while XLE was the ONLY leg in the book that fell (-1.13%). That is the whole rebalance. XLE goes 26-to-20: it was sized as my anchor on a geopolitical-supply-and-inflation premise, but if the Fed is now easing because the labour market is cracking, energy demand is the leg most exposed to that crack, and Friday's tape already showed energy trading as a growth asset rather than a real asset. UUP short goes 3-to-7: last week I explicitly cut it to a 3% token because a hawkish Warsh Fed with September hike risk favoured the near-term rate differential — that exact premise was falsified on Friday, so I restore the leg rather than pretend the reason still holds. COPX goes 12-to-15 because copper is the one holding levered to all three of a weaker dollar, an easing Fed and electrification demand simultaneously. I am NOT adding to GDX despite it being my best performer: the desk note that a dozen short stops fired in the gold complex tells me a large part of Friday's 7% was a crowded-short unwind, and unwind fuel exhausts, so I hold 22% and let the position work rather than chase it. EWZ, EZU and EWJ are untouched — Brazil at PE 9.8 with a 4.1% yield gets the classic EM tailwind from Fed easing that offsets the 25% tariff drag, and Europe and Japan are both sitting at 52-week highs with the Stoxx 600 at records on ~20.8% earnings growth, which is a reason to leave them alone rather than to trade around them. Cash to 7%; at a 4% APY there is no case for holding more when every real-asset leg just got a monetary tailwind.
novelty: Round 3 shares zero names and zero same-direction gross weight with my Round 2 book: Round 2 is 85% long US AI-infrastructure equities (power generation, semi-cap, custom silicon, networking, datacenter thermal) with no shorts, while Round 3 is 86% long non-US and real-asset exposure (energy, gold miners, copper miners, Brazil, eurozone, Japan) plus a 7% short dollar leg — the two books have no overlapping ticker and are driven by opposite macro inputs, since Round 2 wants nominal growth and Round 3 wants a falling real rate and a weaker dollar.

WHAT I LEARNED THAT CHANGED MY MIND: (1) My SMCI short thesis is being contradicted by the issuer itself — SMCI pre-announced strong prelims and the street raised targets; I was holding a squeezing 9% short into a positively pre-announced Aug 11 print, in a tape where 12 of 17 standing orders that ever fired were shorts getting stopped out. (2) ANET, not MU, produced the week's actual fundamental confirmation, and it is my most under-weighted leg. (3) SK Hynix capex is bullish the tool vendor (AMAT) and bearish the commodity (MU) — the shortage is now inducing supply. (4) The hawkish-Warsh-Fed premise on which I cut my dollar short to 3% last week was falsified by the payroll miss.
